newsitem.title: INDIA: Japan's ANA to fly to Delhi.
newsitem.headline: Japan's ANA to fly to Delhi.

text.p: Japan's All Nippon Airways (ANA) on Thursday announced the launch of twice-weekly flights between Delhi and Tokyo.
"We look forward to playing an active role in facilitating the flow of people and goods between Japan, India and Thailand," said ANA senior vice president Koji Yamashita.
Starting on Friday, the airline will operate twice weekly from Delhi via Bangkok to Tokyo, and will offer business and economy class.
ANA's announcement came on the same day as rival Japan Airlines (JAL) resumed weekly service between New Delhi and Kansai International Airport near Osaka, after a four-year interruption.
JAL also began direct weekly service between New Delhi and Tokyo's Narita airport on Thursday, a company statement said.
JAL suspended its New Delhi-Narita service in 1992 due to slack demand.
ANA said it expects 33,000 passengers on its Tokyo-Delhi route in the first year of operation.
"ANA sees tremendous potential in the Indian market," Yamashita said.
"We are confident of the growth potential for traffic in and out of India as we are for the first time in our history opening two new destinations in a single market in a month."
On September 5, ANA launched the first ever twice-weekly service between Bombay and Osaka.
Passenger traffic between India and Japan has grown at the rate of 17 percent annually over the last five years. In 1995, arrivals in India from Japan were 4.3 percent of all arrivals.

"In 1995, the number of Japanese visiting India increased by 23 percent to 52,000, representing the eleventh largest growth for Japanese outbound travel. We hope that our services to Delhi will help further increase these numbers," Yamashita said.
The decision to route the flights through Bangkok reflected the 18 percent annual growth in the number of Indians entering Thailand, as well as the business potential of that sector, he said.
He said ANA was looking to clinch a 12.5 percent seat share in its first year of operations to India and hoped to increase it to 13 percent by next year.
